live_intro: A machine-learning model reproduces SFINCS in about a second. It is a research tool, not a forecast, and it is less reliable outside its training range.

d_caveat: This map is a non-commercial research demo. Depths are modelled, not observed, and the model is not calibrated on any real flood. It floods too much. For official alerts, see IGEBU and Burundi's civil protection. Do not use these numbers to decide on an evacuation.
d_states: Observed: surveyed or mapped by others (OpenStreetMap). Modelled: computed by a model (SFINCS, canopy height estimated by machine learning, model-corrected terrain). Assumed: the result of a rule I applied (population allocation, neighbourhoods, priority rank).
d_what: Three storms simulated with SFINCS at 20 m: maximum water depth, affected buildings and an estimate of the people involved. Lake level: 772.50 m (scenarios 1 and 2) and 772.95 m (scenario 3). “1 in 100 chance each year” means such a storm can come in any year, even two years running.
d_ev_cop: Against the Copernicus EMSN191 model (scenario 4, the same conditions as scenario 3): CSI {csi}, hit rate {hit}, false-alarm ratio {far}. It finds almost everything Copernicus floods, but floods about 40% more area ({model} km² against {ref} km²).
d_ev_gfm: Against Sentinel-1 in 2024: the satellite saw only {obs} km² of flooding against {model} km² modelled. 2024 was mostly a lake rise, so this test does not measure storm-flood quality.
d_ev_sur: The surrogate model reproduces SFINCS with a CSI of {s0} to {s1} on unseen storms and {c0} to {c1} on an unseen catchment.
d_ev_rough: Known defect: the roughness the model reads holds a 4 × 4 km synthetic “forest” test square north of the centre (Mutakura, Ntahangwa, Ngagara, and about half of Buterere and Quartier Industriel). The real canopy is not in the model. Water depths there are less reliable, and these neighbourhoods are among the most affected. The simulations need to be rerun.
d_s1_note: Scenario 1 predates a model fix (curve numbers); the measured effect on the other scenarios is under 1%.
d_datum: The lake level is 772.50 m (EGM2008, the 2024 peak). A press figure of about 777 m is a local gauge reading: do not mix the two.
d_lake: Lake Tanganyika is excluded from areas and colours: the model shows about 2.5 m of water there, which is open water, not flooding.
d_people: People come from WorldPop 2020, shared among buildings by floor area. The estimate can be wrong in informal areas. Counts are rounded and shown per area, never per building. Neighbourhoods are cells around 77 points, not official boundaries.
d_veg: Canopy comes from the Meta and WRI canopy height map (estimated from 2016–2020 satellite images, 1 m), shifted 6 m north and 4 m east to match building footprints, then aggregated to 5 m. Trees are the {n} crowns detected on that map, a lower bound under closed canopy. No species are given. The canopy share per neighbourhood is descriptive.
d_vegflood: On the steep hills above Bujumbura, bare and built-up slopes speed up runoff and open gullies: researchers have mapped over 1,200 landslides and 81 gullies around the city. Trees and ground cover slow runoff and hold soil, mostly in small and moderate storms. This map does not show that planting trees would lower these depths: the model has not been run with different vegetation, and most modelled flooding comes from rivers draining about 1,000 km² of hills outside the canopy map.
d_keys: On the map: arrow keys to pan, + and − to zoom. Keys 1, 2 and 3: change scenario (when focus is on the map or the panel).
